 This edition of the Flatwater Free Press statewide newsletter was delivered on Nov. 6. 
 STATEWIDE NEWSLETTER
 Blue(ish) wave; Eyebrow-raising state spending; Looking for the helpers
 Plus an Election Day extravaganza and news from around Nebraska.
 Matthew Hansen 
 Marcel Shannon, 4, sits in his stroller and waits as his mother, Bennetta, votes in the King Science & Technology Magnet Middle School gym on Election Day. Photo by Rebecca S. Gratz for the Flatwater Free Press Maybe you heard — there was an election this week. 
 Hi, it’s Flatwater editor Matthew Hansen, on my third cup of coffee this morning as I battle through what was and always is an exhilarating and exhausting week in this newsroom and every newsroom in the country. 
 We’ll get to that election in a second. 
 First, I want to highlight a few other stories that Flatwater did this week. I want to do that because they are all great and could be easily missed in the Election Day tumult. 
 Eyebrow raising: This week, Andrew Wegley brought us an eye-opening investigative story about the present and future of small-town hospitals. 
 When Congress passed the “One Big Beautiful Bill” that deeply cuts Medicaid, they did so with a $50 billion infusion for rural health care, ostensibly to protect small-town hospitals from dying in the process. 
 The State of Nebraska is receiving that money, some $218 million, in fact. But a shockingly small amount of it is actually being sent to rural hospitals, a new Flatwater analysis found. 
 Zero, in fact, has gone to Garden County’s only hospital, which is teetering on the brink of closure. At the same time, some $142,000 has gone to a gardener who lists his north Lincoln apartment as his company address and promises to grow “specialty vegetables from Africa and the Caribbean.” 
 This story is a must read from Wegley. 
 Safe harbor at Elk Hills: I adore this story from Emily Wolf, published Thursday. Wolf figured that a gigantic number of Ukrainians who have fled the war now live together in one nondescript apartment building in Elkhorn. 
 She found them, she met them, she let us meet them . She learned about how their tenuous existence inside this country is very much tethered to decisions made by President Donald Trump. 
 And, like Mr. Rogers taught us, she looked for the helpers. She found Nebraskans who are selflessly working to better the lives of their new Ukrainian neighbors. 
 A lovely, important story as Wolf continues her series, “Refuge at Risk.” 
 Mercury says goodbye: Early this week, we had a story that garnered a ton of attention in our biggest city. Flatwater Omaha reporter Jeremy Turley broke the story that Clark Ross, co-owner of beloved bar Mercury and one of the leading advocates for small businesses harmed by streetcar construction, is closing his bar. 
 The story details steps the city and philanthropists have taken to try to help Ross and other small businesses along the construction route. But it also reveals an instance of a city leader discouraging a company from holding a gathering at the bar — a viewpoint that said city leader doubled down on in an interview with Turley. 
 Thank you to our sponsor: I’m so excited to say that, this week, it’s the Walk to End Alzheimer’s. That walk, held in October, drew some 1,500 participants and raised nearly a quarter-million dollars to fund local programs and Alzheimer’s research. 
 I cannot think of a more dastardly disease. I cannot think of a more important hunt for a cure. Read about the guy behind the 2026 walk . And learn more about these walks, which happen across the country and will happen again here next year. 
 Thank you to the Walk to End Alzheimer’s for doing what you do. And thank you for supporting the mission of nonprofit news. 
 Oh, and about that election: This week, really for the first time, Flatwater went hard on election coverage. 
 Before Election Day,Margery Beck brought you a story about how a group of 2020 election deniers may have changed the way people vote in Sarpy County. 
 On Election Day, we ran our first-ever live blog , with reporters and photographers fanning out across metro Omaha. They identified some weirdness around the poll watching — for example, I didn’t think the name Ted Cruz would enter the chat. And they realized, throughout the course of the day, that turnout was really high across the more Democratic-leaning parts of Omaha, giving readers a glimpse of what the election night results would look like before the polls even closed. 
 And then today, our first-two post-election analyses, using the numbers to drive the story. 
 Sarpy County, which along with the rest of the Omaha suburbs is to me kind of the ancestral home of old-school Nebraska Republicanism, swung hard blue on Tuesday. Henry Cordes has the story of what’s happening in Sarpy. 
 And North and South Omaha did indeed turn out in force, galvanized by the immigration crackdown and spiraling costs that are hammering the working class, grassroots organizers and experts said. 
 That turnout explosion aided new Congresswoman Denise Powell as she romped to victory over Brinker Harding. And it aided in the kind-of-stunning defeats of Douglas County’s longtime county attorney and its incumbent county sheriff. Turley, who has been doing it all this week, with the story. 
 I’m really proud of the journalism we committed during Election Week. If you see a Flatwater journalist out and about, buy them a caffeinated beverage or simply thank them. They’re working hard to get you the scoop.   
 See you in Kearney: Central Nebraskans! Don’t forget, on Wednesday, we’re hosting a Happy Hour meet-and-greet in Kearney. Meet our new Tri-Cities reporter, Pierce Gentry, have a beverage on us and tell us your story ideas. Everyone is invited. Excited to see you there. 
 Coming next week: We will break down how Sen. Pete Ricketts prevailed during the blue wave. That story is publishing Monday. 
 Questions wanted: Some of our best story ideas come from readers, and they typically start with a burning question that just cries out for an answer. Have a question that our reporters need to look into? Reach our newsroom at [email protected] . 
 Sincerely, 
 Matthew Hansen, Executive Editor 
 Here’s what we’re into this week: News from around Nebraska
 Every week, we like to share great Nebraska journalism, no matter who made it. Here’s what caught our eye this week: 
 Hey, Lincoln — we have a ton of Flatwater employees running the Good Life Halfsy on Sunday morning, and a cheer station will be set up around Mile 3. I will be there shaking a sign! To get you in the mood, here’s this incredible audio story from The New York Times. What it sounds like to run across the bridge that’s known as the worst part of the New York City Marathon … and then get to the very best part. 
 Remember that fertilizer plant that Vice President JD Vance said was coming to Nebraska during a pre-election speech here? It seems likely to land in Superior, aka SuperTown, where several of my best college friends hail from. But it’s not a done deal yet , reports Nebraska Public Media’s Sami Mirza.
 The Nebraska Legislature got a little bit bluer on Tuesday , with Democrats poised to pick up three crucial seats. It will give them far more power to stop legislation via the filibuster. But Republicans still maintain a firm grip on majority control in the officially nonpartisan Legislature. Story by the Nebraska Examiner’s Zach Wendling.
 The State Board of Education got more Republican, by contrast. Meanwhile, the University of Nebraska’s Board of Regents had some interesting races. Also by Wendling, who was a busy guy this week.
 Lincoln Public Schools has 700 fewer students this year , as the city’s birth rate continues to fall, reports the Journal Star’s Livia Ziskey. (You may need Journal Star subscription info to access this story.)
 Gov. Jim Pillen suggested Friday that a special session of the Legislature is not off the table. Story by The World-Herald’s Josh Reyes. (You may need OWH subscription info to access.)
 State Auditor Mike Foley is wondering why a retirement official is still getting paid by the state. Story by NPM’s Scott Koperski.
